intro.caption: Lesson 4-3 — estimate the percent of a number. Before the weekend sale starts, the crew bets on who can eyeball the closest discount before Hye-jin taps equals on her calculator.

balloons.t: No calculators! Closest mental estimate to the real discount wins the paper trophy.
I bet five sunflower seeds nobody beats Hye-jin.
9% off $198? Round to 10% of $200 and slide the decimal left once!
Smart! 10% is the easiest benchmark. Double it for 20%, halve it for 5%.
25% off $100! Easy — 25% means divide by 25, so $4 off!
Four dollars off a hundred?! Ruben, 25% is ONE QUARTER. Divide by 4!
24% off $122 looks ugly. Can I nudge BOTH numbers to friendly ones?
Yes! Use 25% of $120 — compatible numbers that divide cleanly in your head.
If I give you 25% off an $80 shoe, you only save $3.20. Take it or leave it.
He just divided by 25! Call him out, crew!
Best guesser in the shop! And Sly's $3.20 scam is officially retired.

win.caption: To estimate a percent, round to a benchmark percent (10%, 25%, 50%) and a compatible number. Remember: 25% means one quarter (÷ 4), never ÷ 25.

gates.title: Gate 1 · The 10% Jump
gates.prompt: Use the 10% benchmark and compatible numbers to eyeball these discounts fast.
hints: Conceptual: 10% is one tenth of a number, so every 10% jump moves the decimal point one place left.
Procedural: round the percent to 10% or 20%, and round the price to a nearby multiple of 10.

items.label: 9% off $198. Round to 10% of $200. Discount ≈ ($)
items.aria: estimated discount for ten percent of two hundred dollars

fb.msg: $2 is 1% of $200. For 10%, move the decimal point one place left, not two.
$200 is the full rounded price, not 10% of it.

items.fbDefault: Move the decimal point one place left on 200 to find 10%.

items.q: A hoodie is $78 and 21% off. Which compatible numbers give the closest quick estimate?

options.fb: 100 is far from 78. $80 is much closer and still easy for 20%.
78 is much closer to 80 than to 70.

gates.pass: About $20 and $16! Tasha is leading the guessing game.

gates.title: Gate 2 · Quarters and Halves
gates.prompt: Fix Ruben's 25% mistake, then use 50% to estimate a half-price deal.
hints: Conceptual: 50% means one half (divide by 2), and 25% means one quarter (divide by 4), never divide by 25.
Procedural: round the price to a friendly number, then divide by 4 for 25% or by 2 for 50%.

items.q: A $100 sneaker is 25% off. Ruben says "$100 ÷ 25 = $4 off!" What is the real discount?

options.fb: 25% means 25 out of 100 (1/4), not divide by 25! Divide $100 by 4.
$75 is the sale price you pay, not the 25% discount.

options.t: $25 off, because 25% is 1/4 so divide by 4

options.fb: Half is 50%. 25% is one quarter, which is $25.

items.label: Joggers are $82 and 48% off. Estimate with 50% of $80. Discount ≈ ($)
items.aria: estimated discount for fifty percent of eighty dollars

fb.msg: $20 is 25% of $80. For 50%, take half of $80.
$80 is the full rounded price, not half of it.

items.fbDefault: 50% is one half. What is half of $80?

gates.pass: $25 off and $40 off! Ruben promises never to divide by 25 for 25% again.

gates.title: Gate 3 · Compatible Numbers
gates.prompt: Nudge both the percent and the price to friendly compatible numbers, then check if your estimate is high or low.
hints: Conceptual: rounding both numbers up makes an estimate slightly higher than exact; rounding down makes it lower.
Procedural: pick a nearby benchmark percent and a price that divides cleanly by it.

items.label: Estimate 24% of $122 using 25% of $120. Discount ≈ ($)
items.aria: estimated discount for twenty five percent of one hundred twenty dollars

fb.msg: $60 is 50% of $120. 25% is one quarter, so divide by 4.

items.q: Cole estimates 19% of $49 using 20% of $50 = $10. Is his estimate a little high or a little low?

options.t: A little high, because both 19% and $49 rounded up
A little low, because both rounded down
options.fb: 19% went UP to 20% and $49 went UP to $50.

options.t: Exact, because rounding never changes the answer
options.fb: Rounding both numbers up makes the estimate slightly higher than exact.

options.t: Half too big, because 20% is half
options.fb: 20% is one fifth, and 20% is very close to 19%.

gates.pass: About $30, and Cole spotted the rounding direction! One boss round left.

gates.title: Boss Gate · Win the Guess
gates.prompt: Two rapid estimation rounds plus Sly's 25% trick. Beat the calculator!
hints: Conceptual: 10% moves the decimal left one place; 25% divides by 4.
Procedural: round to compatible numbers first, then apply the benchmark.

items.label: Round 1 · Estimate 11% of $295 using 10% of $300. ($)
items.aria: estimated ten percent of three hundred dollars

fb.msg: $3 is 1% of $300. For 10%, move the decimal one place left.
$300 is the whole price, not 10% of it.

items.fbDefault: 10% of $300 moves the decimal point one place left.

items.label: Round 2 · Estimate 26% of $197 using 25% of $200. ($)
items.aria: estimated twenty five percent of two hundred dollars

fb.msg: 25% means one quarter (divide by 4), NOT divide by 25!

items.q: Tiebreaker · Sly claims 25% of $80 is $3.20 ("just divide 80 by 25!"). What is the real answer?

options.fb: 25% of $100 is $25, but here the whole is $80.

gates.pass: DING! $30, $50, and $20! Cole takes the paper trophy and Sly walks away empty-handed.

journal.heading: Lesson 4-3 — what the guessing contest taught us
rows: Move the decimal point one place left: 10% of $200 = $20. Build 20% or 5% from there.
50% is half (÷ 2). 25% is one quarter (÷ 4) — NEVER divide by 25!
Nudge both numbers to friendly ones: 24% of $122 ≈ 25% of $120 = $30.
If both numbers rounded up, your estimate sits a little above the exact answer.
journal.quote: "25% means a quarter, not divide by 25. Write that on your forehead, Ruben." — Kicks
